brief: UBS chief economist Arend Kapteyn says the bank now models how equities would react to a shock (an oil spike, tariffs, AI disappointment) before it models the economy, reversing the usual economist-to-strategist sequencing, because US household equity and mutual fund holdings are near 200% of GDP, up from 108% before the dot-com bust, plus another 110% of GDP in pension entitlements, so a 10% market move shifts household wealth by roughly 20% of GDP. Applying assumed spending propensities (about 6 cents per extra housing-wealth dollar, 3 cents per extra equity-wealth dollar) produces a wealth effect UBS puts at 0.9 percentage points of GDP over the past four quarters, almost 3x its pre-pandemic average and twice its dot-com-era level, because equity and mutual fund holdings have grown by nearly 70% of GDP since Q1 2023 alone, as much as housing wealth gained over nine years before the financial crisis. UBS notes the same math runs in reverse: a 20% bear market could cut consumption by about 1.2% of GDP, close to the entire wealth effect UBS calculates today, and because much of that equity wealth sits in a handful of AI names, an AI disappointment could be enough to trigger it.
